subject: biology
title: D4.2 Stability and change
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: D4.2 Stability and change — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic D4.2.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D4.2 Stability and change, guide topic D4.2.
final_note: You worked through D4.2 Stability and change — 15 guide statements.

concepts.def: The property of a natural ecosystem by which it persists over long periods, keeping the same overall structure and type of community, even though the populations within it fluctuate and individual organisms are continually replaced. Stability is a property of the ecosystem as a whole, not of its individual members.

Evidence that a type of ecosystem has occupied a region continuously through geological time, obtained from dated sediment cores, fossil pollen, fossil leaves and wood, and fossil animals. Such evidence indicates that some ecosystems have persisted for millions of years: tropical rainforest in parts of the Amazon basin and northern Australia is estimated to have persisted for tens of millions of years, and the Namib Desert of southern Africa is estimated to have been arid for around 55 million years.

concepts.term: Supply of energy as a requirement for stability
concepts.def: A continuous input of energy, almost always light from the Sun captured by producers in photosynthesis, that an ecosystem needs in order to remain stable. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat at every trophic level, so it cannot be recycled and must be supplied continuously.

concepts.term: Recycling of nutrients as a requirement for stability
concepts.def: The return of chemical elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus from dead organic matter and waste to the abiotic environment, mainly through decomposition by saprotrophic bacteria and fungi, so that producers can take them up again. Because the supply of nutrients in an ecosystem is finite, this recycling is essential for the ecosystem to persist.

concepts.term: Genetic diversity as a requirement for stability
concepts.def: The variety of alleles present in the populations of an ecosystem. A genetically diverse population is likely to contain some individuals with alleles that allow survival when a new disease, pest or change in conditions arrives, so the population and the ecosystem that depends on it are less likely to collapse.

The range of values of a climatic variable such as temperature, rainfall or humidity within which the organisms of an ecosystem can survive and reproduce. An ecosystem can remain stable while climatic variables fluctuate, provided the fluctuations stay within the tolerance levels of the species present.

A threshold beyond which a small further change in a variable causes a large, rapid and often irreversible change in the state of an ecosystem. Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest is a possible example: beyond some minimum area of forest, moisture recycling may fail and forest may be replaced by drier savanna-like vegetation.

concepts.term: Moisture recycling by the Amazon rainforest
concepts.def: The generation of atmospheric water vapour by transpiration from a very large area of trees. The water vapour cools the air as it evaporates, drives air flows across the region, and condenses to give rainfall on which the forest itself depends. A large area of intact forest is needed to maintain these processes, and the minimum area that is sufficient is uncertain.

The change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of its original value: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100. A decrease gives a negative value. The extent of deforestation is assessed as the percentage change from the original area of forest.

A small, enclosed experimental ecosystem set up as a model of a natural ecosystem, containing producers, consumers and decomposers with abiotic components such as water, sediment or soil, so that the effect of a variable on stability can be investigated. Aquatic or microbial mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones.

concepts.term: Sealed mesocosm as a system closed to matter but open to energy
concepts.def: A mesocosm in a sealed glass vessel is preferable to one in an open tank because entry and exit of matter is prevented, so nutrients must be recycled within it, while energy transfer remains possible: light enters through the glass and heat leaves. Care and maintenance of mesocosms should follow IB experimental guidelines, so that organisms do not suffer.

A species that has a disproportionately large effect on the structure of its community relative to its abundance or biomass. Removal of a keystone species can change the whole community and risks ecosystem collapse. Examples include sea otters in kelp forests, the starfish Pisaster on rocky shores, wolves in Yellowstone and beavers.

The set of species present in a community and their relative abundances and trophic relationships. A keystone species maintains community structure, for example by preventing one competitor or herbivore from dominating; its removal can lead to a cascade of changes through the food web.

A resource harvested from a natural ecosystem that is replaced by natural processes such as growth and reproduction, for example timber or nuts from wild trees and fish from the sea. A renewable resource can still be depleted if it is harvested faster than it is replaced.

Harvesting a renewable resource at a rate lower than the rate at which it is replaced by growth and reproduction, so that the stock does not decline and the harvest can continue indefinitely. Harvesting above the replacement rate depletes the stock and can lead to collapse.

Judging whether harvesting is sustainable by comparing harvest rate with replacement rate, using indicators such as the size of the stock, trends in the catch or yield, the effort needed to obtain it, and the age structure of the population. For a marine fish such as Atlantic cod, a rising fishing effort for the same catch and a fall in the mean age of fish caught indicate over-harvesting. For a terrestrial plant such as the Brazil nut tree, the presence of seedlings and young trees indicates that harvesting of nuts is leaving enough seeds for replacement.

The extent to which a system of farming can continue indefinitely without degrading the resources it depends on. Factors to consider include soil erosion, leaching of nutrients, the supply of fertilizers and other inputs, pollution due to agrochemicals, and the carbon footprint of the farming.

The washing of soluble substances, such as nitrate and phosphate from fertilizers, down through the soil by rainwater or irrigation into groundwater, streams, lakes and the sea. Leaching both depletes soil nutrients and pollutes water.

The total greenhouse gas emissions attributable to a farming system, including carbon dioxide from fuel used by machinery and from the manufacture of fertilizers and other inputs, methane from livestock, nitrous oxide released from fertilized soils, and carbon dioxide from clearing land.

The enrichment of a body of water with nutrients, especially nitrate and phosphate leached from fertilized farmland. The nutrients cause rapid growth of algae (an algal bloom); the algae then die and are decomposed by aerobic saprotrophic bacteria, whose respiration lowers the concentration of dissolved oxygen so that fish and other aerobic organisms die. Eutrophication affects lakes, rivers and coastal marine waters.

The quantity of dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic microorganisms as they decompose the organic matter in a sample of water, usually measured over five days. A high BOD indicates a large amount of decomposable organic matter and therefore a high rate of oxygen removal from the water; eutrophication increases BOD.

The increase in the concentration of a persistent toxin in the tissues of organisms at each successive trophic level of a food chain. A consumer takes in the toxin from every prey organism it eats and, because the toxin is not broken down or excreted, it accumulates, so top consumers carry the highest concentrations.

concepts.term: DDT as an example of biomagnification
concepts.def: An insecticide that is fat-soluble and persistent in the environment. DDT sprayed on crops and wetlands entered food chains and became concentrated in birds of prey and fish-eating birds, where it caused thinning of eggshells and breeding failure. Its use was banned in many countries from the 1970s.

concepts.term: Mercury as an example of biomagnification
concepts.def: A toxic metal released by industry, mining and the burning of coal. In water and sediments bacteria convert mercury to methylmercury, which is retained in tissues and biomagnified along aquatic food chains, reaching high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna and swordfish. People eating contaminated fish and shellfish at Minamata in Japan suffered severe nervous system damage.

Macroplastics are visible items of plastic debris such as bags, bottles and fishing nets; microplastics are fragments smaller than about 5 mm, produced by the breakdown of macroplastics or manufactured as fibres and beads. Macroplastics harm marine animals by entanglement and by blocking the gut when swallowed; microplastics are ingested by filter feeders and other animals, can carry adsorbed pollutants, and pass along food chains.

Plastics remain in the environment for very long periods because they are not biodegradable: decomposers lack enzymes able to break down these synthetic polymers. Plastics fragment into ever smaller pieces but the material is not removed. Clear communication of research on the effects of plastics on marine life changed public perception globally and drove measures to reduce plastic pollution.

Restoration of natural processes in a degraded ecosystem so that it can maintain itself with little further intervention. Methods include reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species, re-establishment of connectivity between habitats over large areas, and minimization of human impact, including by ecological management such as removing livestock or controlling introduced species.

The degree to which areas of habitat are linked so that organisms can move between them. Re-establishing connectivity by corridors and by removing barriers allows animals to migrate, disperse and breed across a large area, maintaining population sizes and genetic diversity.

A reserve of more than 1000 hectares on Banks Peninsula, New Zealand, where former farmland has been allowed to return to native forest since 1987 by minimal interference. Grazing livestock were removed and introduced browsing mammals are controlled, but the invasive shrub gorse was left in place as a nurse canopy: native tree seedlings grow up through it and shade it out, and native forest has regenerated naturally.

The process by which the community in an area changes over time, with one community being replaced by another, until a relatively stable climax community is reached. Succession can be triggered by changes in the abiotic environment, such as a volcanic eruption or glacial retreat, and by biotic factors, such as organisms altering the soil or shading the ground.

Primary succession begins in an area where no soil and no previous community exist, such as bare rock or sand exposed by a retreating glacier or created by a volcano. Secondary succession begins where a previous community has been removed but soil remains, for example after a fire or the abandonment of farmland.

The first community to colonise bare ground in primary succession, typically lichens, mosses and small hardy plants that can tolerate the lack of soil, water and nutrients. Pioneers begin to form soil by trapping particles and adding organic matter, changing the environment so that other species can establish.

As primary succession proceeds, the size of plants increases, the amount of primary production increases, species diversity increases, food webs become more complex and the amount of nutrient cycling increases, as soil depth and organic content build up.

A pattern in which a community passes repeatedly through a cycle of phases rather than settling into a single unchanging climax community. In heather moorland, heather plants pass through pioneer, building, mature and degenerate phases; when old plants die back, the gap is colonised by lichens, mosses and other plants before heather seedlings re-establish and the cycle begins again.

The relatively stable community that ecological succession tends to lead to under a given set of environmental conditions, such as temperate deciduous woodland or tropical rainforest. Its composition depends on the climate and soil of the area.

Prevention of the development of the climax community by a human influence, so that the community is held at an earlier stage of succession. Grazing by farm livestock, which removes tree and shrub seedlings and keeps land as grassland, and drainage of wetlands for agriculture are examples; if the influence is removed, succession can resume.

mcqs.q: What evidence indicates that an ecosystem has persisted, and so shown stability, for millions of years?
options: Fossil pollen from dated layers of sediment shows the same type of plant community persisting through geological time.
The oldest individual trees now growing in the ecosystem have been dated at several thousand years old.
Census data show that the population size of every species has stayed exactly constant from year to year.
The ecosystem has a high rate of primary production and supports a very large number of species.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
mcqs.explain: Dated sediment cores containing fossil pollen, leaves and animals record the community present at each time. Where the same type of community appears throughout, the ecosystem has shown continuity, in some cases for millions of years.
rationales: Dated sediment cores containing fossil pollen, leaves and animals record the community present at each time. Where the same type of community appears throughout, the ecosystem has shown continuity, in some cases for millions of years.

A student who takes the age of living individuals as the age of the ecosystem picks this. A few thousand years is far short of millions, and no individual lives that long; the evidence comes from fossils in dated sediments.
A student who thinks stability means no change picks this. Populations in a stable ecosystem fluctuate; it is the persistence of the same type of community that shows stability.
A student who equates stability with productivity and richness picks this. Stability is persistence over time, and sparsely populated deserts have persisted for as long as any rainforest.

mcqs.q: Sediment cores from a desert basin contain pollen in every layer. The layers have been dated to span the last 30 million years, and the deepest layers contain pollen of the same drought-adapted plant families as the surface layers. What is the best conclusion from this evidence?
options: The region cannot have supported a stable ecosystem for so long, because a desert is too harsh to persist for millions of years.
A desert ecosystem has persisted in this region for tens of millions of years, so it has shown long-term stability.
The plants whose pollen is in the deepest layers must still be alive today for the ecosystem to count as stable.
The ecosystem was not stable, because the numbers of each species must have varied over 30 million years.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
mcqs.explain: The same type of community, identified from its pollen, is present throughout 30 million years of dated sediment. That is direct evidence of an ecosystem persisting over a very long period, which is what stability means.
rationales: A student who thinks only productive ecosystems can be stable picks this. The evidence shows precisely that the desert did persist; harshness of conditions does not prevent continuity.

The same type of community, identified from its pollen, is present throughout 30 million years of dated sediment. That is direct evidence of an ecosystem persisting over a very long period, which is what stability means.

A student who thinks persistence must be shown by living individuals picks this. No plant lives for 30 million years; continuity of the community type, not survival of individuals, is the evidence of stability.
A student who equates stability with constant populations picks this. Population sizes fluctuate in every ecosystem; the persistence of the same kind of community is what shows stability.

mcqs.q: Which set of conditions is required for an ecosystem to remain stable?
options: Recycling of both energy and nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, large population sizes and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables that are held perfectly constant.
mcqs.specStatementText: What an ecosystem needs to stay stable
mcqs.explain: These are the four requirements the guide lists. Energy must be supplied continuously because it is lost as heat; nutrients must be recycled because their supply is finite; genetic diversity allows populations to survive change; and climate must stay within the tolerance of the species present.
rationales: A student who thinks energy cycles like carbon or nitrogen picks this. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat at each trophic level, so it must be supplied continuously and cannot be recycled.

A student who thinks population size can stand in for genetic diversity picks this. A large but genetically uniform population can be destroyed by a single disease; it is diversity of alleles that gives resilience.

These are the four requirements the guide lists. Energy must be supplied continuously because it is lost as heat; nutrients must be recycled because their supply is finite; genetic diversity allows populations to survive change; and climate must stay within the tolerance of the species present.
A student who reads 'stable' as 'constant' picks this. Climatic variables fluctuate in every ecosystem; the requirement is that they remain within the tolerance levels of the organisms.

mcqs.q: A plantation forest consists of a single tree species, all grown from cuttings of one parent tree, so the trees are genetically almost identical. A fungal disease that kills this species arrives. Which statement about the stability of this forest is correct?
options: It is as stable as a natural forest, because stability depends on the number of trees, not on their genetic variation.
It will remain stable, because the energy in the trees killed by the fungus is recycled to support new tree growth.
It is stable because a forest is a highly productive ecosystem with a large rate of photosynthesis per hectare.
It is vulnerable to collapse because few or no trees carry alleles that give resistance to the disease.
mcqs.specStatementText: What an ecosystem needs to stay stable
mcqs.explain: Genetic diversity is a requirement for stability. In a genetically uniform population, no individuals are likely to carry resistance alleles, so the disease can kill almost every tree and the ecosystem that depends on them collapses.
rationales: A student who confuses population size with genetic diversity picks this. However many trees there are, if all are susceptible the disease can destroy them all.

A student who thinks energy is recycled picks this. Energy in dead trees is released as heat by decomposers; only nutrients are recycled, and recycling nutrients cannot replace a population with no resistance.
A student who equates stability with productivity picks this. High production does not protect a genetically uniform population from a disease to which none of its members is resistant.

Genetic diversity is a requirement for stability. In a genetically uniform population, no individuals are likely to carry resistance alleles, so the disease can kill almost every tree and the ecosystem that depends on them collapses.

mcqs.q: In 1970 the area of a rainforest was 4 000 000 km². By 2020 the area was 3 320 000 km². What is the percentage change in the area of forest?
mcqs.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
mcqs.explain: Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = (3 320 000 − 4 000 000) ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −680 000 ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −17.0%. The negative sign shows a decrease from the original area of forest.
rationales: Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = (3 320 000 − 4 000 000) ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −680 000 ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = −17.0%. The negative sign shows a decrease from the original area of forest.
A student who divides the change by the final area picks this: 680 000 ÷ 3 320 000 × 100 = 20.5%. Percentage change is always expressed relative to the original value, 4 000 000 km².

A student who calculates the percentage of the original forest that remains, 3 320 000 ÷ 4 000 000 × 100 = 83%, and reports it as the size of the decrease picks this. The question asks for the change, which is 83% − 100% = −17%.
A student who misplaces the decimal point when converting the fraction −0.17 to a percentage picks this. Multiplying by 100 gives −17%, not −1.7%.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly explains the link between the area of the Amazon rainforest and the rainfall it receives?
options: Rain over the forest comes from water evaporated from the Atlantic Ocean, so the area of forest has little effect on the rainfall.
Transpiration from a large area of trees adds water vapour to the air, which cools, drives air flows and returns as rain over the forest.
Every hectare of forest contributes a fixed share of the rainfall, so rainfall falls in exact proportion to the area of forest that is cleared.
Scientists have established that rainfall stays the same until exactly 20% of the forest has been cleared, and then declines sharply.
mcqs.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
mcqs.explain: The forest generates a large proportion of its own rainfall. Water vapour from transpiration produces cooling, air flows and rainfall, so a large area of forest is needed to keep these processes going.
rationales: A student who pictures the water cycle as sea-to-land only picks this. Ocean evaporation supplies some rain, but transpiration from the forest itself is a major source of the water vapour that falls as rain over the Amazon.

The forest generates a large proportion of its own rainfall. Water vapour from transpiration produces cooling, air flows and rainfall, so a large area of forest is needed to keep these processes going.

A student who expects a linear response picks this. Moisture recycling may continue until a threshold area is lost and then fail rapidly; this possible tipping point is why the relationship is not simply proportional.

A student who treats an estimate as an exact known value picks this. Some researchers have suggested a threshold in the region of 20–25% deforestation, but the minimum area of forest needed is uncertain.

mcqs.q: Different research groups have estimated that the Amazon rainforest could reach a tipping point when 20%, 25% or 40% of its original area has been deforested. About 17% has been cleared so far. What does this range of estimates indicate?
options: Only one of the estimates can be correct, so nothing can be concluded until the other two have been shown to be wrong.
Rainfall must already have fallen by 17%, in proportion to the area cleared, so there is no threshold left to estimate.
The minimum area of forest needed to maintain moisture recycling is uncertain, so the tipping point could be close.
Rainfall over the forest comes from the ocean, so deforestation cannot affect it and no tipping point can exist.
mcqs.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
mcqs.explain: The estimates differ because models and assumptions differ, which is exactly the uncertainty the guide describes. Since the lowest estimate is only a few percentage points above the area already cleared, the tipping point may be near, which argues for caution.
rationales: A student who thinks a threshold is a precisely known value picks this. A range of estimates is informative in itself: it shows that the threshold is uncertain and that the lowest estimate is uncomfortably close to current deforestation.
A student who assumes a linear response picks this. The concern about a tipping point is precisely that rainfall may be largely maintained until a threshold is crossed and then fall abruptly.

The estimates differ because models and assumptions differ, which is exactly the uncertainty the guide describes. Since the lowest estimate is only a few percentage points above the area already cleared, the tipping point may be near, which argues for caution.
A student who thinks the forest does not generate its own rain picks this. Transpiration from the forest supplies much of the water vapour that returns as rain, so loss of forest can reduce rainfall.

mcqs.q: Why is a sealed glass vessel preferable to an open tank for a mesocosm used to investigate ecosystem stability?
options: It forms a completely closed system, so neither matter nor energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
The lid can be removed briefly each day to replace the oxygen that the organisms inside have used up.
It reproduces the natural ecosystem exactly, so any result obtained can be applied directly to the real ecosystem.
Matter cannot enter or leave the vessel, but light can still enter and heat can still leave.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
mcqs.explain: Sealing makes the mesocosm closed to matter, so nutrients must be recycled within it as in a stable ecosystem, while the glass allows energy transfer: light enters to drive photosynthesis and heat leaves.
rationales: A student who thinks sealing shuts out energy as well as matter picks this. Glass transmits light, so energy enters continuously; only matter is prevented from entering or leaving.

A student who thinks oxygen must be supplied from outside picks this. In a balanced mesocosm oxygen released by photosynthesis is recycled through respiration, and opening the vessel would defeat the purpose of sealing it.

A student who thinks a model is an exact copy picks this. A mesocosm is a simplified model; sealing it does not make it identical to a natural ecosystem, and its results must be interpreted with caution.

Sealing makes the mesocosm closed to matter, so nutrients must be recycled within it as in a stable ecosystem, while the glass allows energy transfer: light enters to drive photosynthesis and heat leaves.

mcqs.q: A class plans to use mesocosms to investigate the effect of light intensity on ecosystem stability. Which design is most likely to succeed and to follow IB experimental guidelines?
options: Sealed glass jars containing pond water, algae, small aquatic invertebrates and sediment, placed at different distances from a lamp for several weeks.
Open terraria containing soil, plants and a small lizard, placed at different distances from a lamp, since a terrestrial model is more realistic.
Open tanks of pond water and algae with an air pump running in each, so that the organisms do not run out of oxygen during the investigation.
A single large sealed aquarium containing fish, because a bigger and more realistic model gives results that apply directly to real lakes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
mcqs.explain: Aquatic mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones, sealing prevents exchange of matter while light still enters, and small invertebrates in pond water can be kept without causing suffering, in line with IB guidelines.
rationales: Aquatic mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones, sealing prevents exchange of matter while light still enters, and small invertebrates in pond water can be kept without causing suffering, in line with IB guidelines.

A student who equates realism with size and animals picks this. Terrestrial mesocosms are less likely to succeed, and exposing a vertebrate to treatments that may harm it does not follow IB experimental guidelines.

A student who thinks oxygen must be supplied from outside picks this. Photosynthesis by the algae supplies the oxygen; an open, aerated tank allows matter to enter and leave, so it no longer tests whether the system can sustain itself.

A student who thinks a model reproduces reality exactly picks this. One vessel cannot test the effect of a variable, and no mesocosm, however large, gives results that transfer directly to a natural lake.

mcqs.q: Sea otters make up a tiny fraction of the biomass of a kelp forest. Where otters were hunted to extinction, sea urchins multiplied and grazed the kelp down to bare rock, and the fish, seals and seabirds that depended on the kelp disappeared. What does this show about sea otters?
options: They cannot be a keystone species, because a keystone species is one contributing most of the community's biomass.
They are a keystone species, because their effect on community structure is far greater than their abundance suggests.
Their removal should only have affected the urchins they ate, so the loss of fish and seabirds must have had a different cause.
The kelp forest was not a stable ecosystem, since a stable ecosystem does not change when a species is removed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Keystone species hold the community together
mcqs.explain: A keystone species has a disproportionate impact on community structure relative to its abundance. Otters control urchin numbers; without them the urchins destroy the kelp and the whole community collapses.
rationales: A student who thinks keystone means dominant or most abundant picks this. The defining feature is disproportionate impact, and sea otters are the classic example of a keystone species with small biomass.

A keystone species has a disproportionate impact on community structure relative to its abundance. Otters control urchin numbers; without them the urchins destroy the kelp and the whole community collapses.

A student who traces effects one step along a food chain picks this. The urchin increase destroyed the kelp, and the loss of kelp removed the habitat of fish, seals and seabirds: a cascade through the food web.
A student who thinks stability means immunity to any change picks this. Stable ecosystems depend on their keystone species; the guide's point is that removing one risks ecosystem collapse.

mcqs.q: A stock of Atlantic cod has a biomass of 200 000 tonnes. Each year, growth of the fish and recruitment of young fish add 15% to the biomass, while natural mortality removes 5% of it. What is the annual rate of replacement of the stock, below which the catch must stay for harvesting to be sustainable? The rate of replacement is the net change in biomass from these processes.
options: 10 000 tonnes
30 000 tonnes
20 000 tonnes
40 000 tonnes
mcqs.specStatementText: Is the harvest sustainable?
mcqs.explain: Net replacement = additions − natural losses = 15% − 5% = 10% of 200 000 tonnes = 20 000 tonnes per year. A catch below this leaves the biomass unchanged or rising, so harvesting is sustainable.
rationales: A student who thinks the harvest can take the fish that would have died naturally picks the 5% mortality figure. Natural deaths are a loss from the stock, not a surplus available for catching.
A student who counts only the additions picks 15% of 200 000 tonnes. Natural mortality removes 5% of the biomass each year and must be subtracted to give the net rate of replacement.
Net replacement = additions − natural losses = 15% − 5% = 10% of 200 000 tonnes = 20 000 tonnes per year. A catch below this leaves the biomass unchanged or rising, so harvesting is sustainable.

A student who adds natural mortality to the growth, as though fish that would die anyway could be harvested as well, picks 20% of 200 000 tonnes. Natural mortality reduces the stock; it does not add to what can be taken.

mcqs.q: Records for a cod fishery show that the annual catch stayed close to 250 000 tonnes for 20 years. Over the same period the number of fishing days needed to land that catch doubled, and the mean age of the cod caught fell from 8 years to 4 years. What do these data indicate?
options: Harvesting is sustainable, because the catch has remained constant for two decades and so the stock must be replacing itself.
Harvesting is sustainable, because cod are a renewable resource that reproduce each year and so cannot be depleted by fishing.
The fall in the mean age of the catch cannot affect replacement, because the reproductive rate of any species is a fixed value.
The stock is being harvested unsustainably: more effort is needed for the same catch and few fish now survive to old age.
mcqs.specStatementText: Is the harvest sustainable?
mcqs.explain: A constant catch obtained with doubled effort means catch per unit effort has halved, so the stock has declined. A falling mean age shows that fish are being removed before they grow old, reducing the breeding stock. Both indicate harvesting above the replacement rate.
rationales: A student who judges sustainability from the catch alone picks this. The catch has been maintained only by doubling effort and by taking younger fish, which are signs of a declining stock.

A student who thinks renewable means inexhaustible picks this. A renewable resource is depleted whenever the rate of harvesting exceeds the rate of replacement, and the effort and age data show this is happening.

A student who thinks replacement rate is fixed picks this. Replacement depends on the number of mature fish left to breed; removing fish at younger ages reduces the breeding stock and so reduces replacement.

A constant catch obtained with doubled effort means catch per unit effort has halved, so the stock has declined. A falling mean age shows that fish are being removed before they grow old, reducing the breeding stock. Both indicate harvesting above the replacement rate.

mcqs.q: Which practice increases the sustainability of agriculture on a farm?
options: Applying extra inorganic fertilizer every year so that all the nutrients lost by leaching are replaced.
Growing cover crops between harvests so that the soil is protected from erosion and less nitrate is leached away.
Ploughing sloping fields deeply each year, because soil is replaced by weathering as fast as it is lost.
Replacing manure with manufactured nitrogen fertilizer, since the fertilizer adds nothing to the farm's carbon footprint.
mcqs.specStatementText: What makes farming unsustainable
mcqs.explain: Soil erosion and leaching of nutrients are two of the factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture. Plant cover holds the soil, takes up nitrate that would otherwise leach, and reduces the need for fertilizer inputs.
rationales: A student who thinks more fertilizer means more sustainability picks this. Fertilizer beyond what the crop takes up is itself leached, pollutes water and carries a large carbon footprint from its manufacture.

Soil erosion and leaching of nutrients are two of the factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture. Plant cover holds the soil, takes up nitrate that would otherwise leach, and reduces the need for fertilizer inputs.
A student who thinks soil regenerates quickly picks this. Soil forms over centuries, and bare ploughed slopes lose it rapidly to erosion, which permanently reduces the land's capacity to grow crops.

A student who thinks carbon footprint means only fuel burned on the farm picks this. Manufacturing nitrogen fertilizer uses large amounts of energy from natural gas, so it adds substantially to the carbon footprint.

mcqs.q: Nitrate and phosphate leached from farmland enter a lake. Which sequence of events leads to the death of fish in the lake?
options: Fertilizer enters the lake → fish absorb nitrate across their gills → it poisons them → fish die
Algal bloom → algae die → BOD falls as the algae decay → less oxygen dissolves in the water → fish suffocate
Algal bloom → algae die → aerobic bacteria decompose them → dissolved oxygen falls → fish suffocate
Algal bloom → light is blocked → submerged plants and algae die → fish have nothing to eat → fish starve
mcqs.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
mcqs.explain: Nutrients cause an algal bloom; when the algae die, saprotrophic bacteria decompose them using aerobic respiration, which raises biochemical oxygen demand and depletes dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aerobic animals die.
rationales: A student who thinks the fertilizer is directly toxic picks this. At the concentrations involved nitrate does not poison fish; the deaths are caused by lack of oxygen after the bloom decomposes.

A student who confuses BOD with dissolved oxygen picks this. Decay of the algae raises BOD, because bacteria demand oxygen to decompose the organic matter; it is the dissolved oxygen concentration that falls.

Nutrients cause an algal bloom; when the algae die, saprotrophic bacteria decompose them using aerobic respiration, which raises biochemical oxygen demand and depletes dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aerobic animals die.
A student who reasons only through food chains picks this. Fish in a eutrophic lake die of oxygen depletion, usually suddenly and in large numbers, not of starvation.

mcqs.q: Water was sampled at three points on a river: A, upstream of a farm; B, 2 km downstream of the farm's drainage outlet; and C, 15 km downstream. Nitrate concentration (mg dm⁻³) was 1 at A, 12 at B and 3 at C. BOD (mg dm⁻³) was 2 at A, 14 at B and 4 at C. The number of fish species found was 8 at A, 1 at B and 6 at C. Which explanation fits these data?
options: Algae stimulated by the nitrate at B released extra oxygen by photosynthesis, so the fish must have been lost for another reason.
The BOD of 14 at B shows that the water there holds the most oxygen, so lack of oxygen cannot explain the loss of fish there.
The nitrate at 12 mg dm⁻³ is directly toxic to fish, which by itself explains why only one fish species was found at B.
Nitrate at B caused an algal bloom whose decomposition raised BOD and removed oxygen, so fish were lost.
mcqs.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
mcqs.explain: Leached nitrate is highest just below the outlet, and the high BOD there shows a large amount of decomposing organic matter, the dead algae. Oxygen depletion explains the loss of fish species at B, and the partial recovery at C as nutrients are diluted and used up.
rationales: A student who thinks an algal bloom enriches the water with oxygen picks this. Whatever the algae produced while alive, their decomposition consumes far more oxygen, as the high BOD at B shows.

A student who reads BOD as the amount of oxygen in the water picks this. BOD is the oxygen that decomposers will consume; a high value means oxygen is being removed rapidly, so B is the site most likely to be short of oxygen.

A student who thinks leached fertilizer poisons fish picks this. Nitrate at this level is not directly lethal to fish; it drives eutrophication, and the fish are lost because decomposition of the bloom removes oxygen.

Leached nitrate is highest just below the outlet, and the high BOD there shows a large amount of decomposing organic matter, the dead algae. Oxygen depletion explains the loss of fish species at B, and the partial recovery at C as nutrients are diluted and used up.

mcqs.q: In a study of an estuary, DDT concentrations were measured in parts per million (ppm): water 0.00005, plankton 0.04, small fish 0.5, larger predatory fish 2, fish-eating birds 25. Which statement explains this pattern?
options: DDT is fat-soluble and not excreted, so each consumer retains the DDT from all its prey and the concentration rises at each trophic level.
Birds live longer than fish, so the pattern is due only to each bird having had more years in which to accumulate DDT.
Each organism absorbed DDT directly from the water, so the birds must have been exposed to more contaminated water.
Birds at the top of the food chain eat the greatest mass of food, so they take in the largest total amount of DDT.
mcqs.specStatementText: Biomagnification: DDT and mercury
mcqs.explain: This is biomagnification. The toxin taken in with every prey item is retained in fatty tissue, so a consumer's tissues hold a higher concentration than its food; over four trophic levels the concentration rose about half a million times above that in the water.
rationales: This is biomagnification. The toxin taken in with every prey item is retained in fatty tissue, so a consumer's tissues hold a higher concentration than its food; over four trophic levels the concentration rose about half a million times above that in the water.

A student who confuses biomagnification with accumulation over a lifetime picks this. Longevity contributes, but the step-up occurs at every trophic level, including from plankton to short-lived small fish.
A student who thinks pollutants are taken up only from the surroundings picks this. All these organisms live in or beside the same water; the difference comes from DDT concentrated in food.

A student who confuses total intake with concentration picks this. Eating a large mass of prey is not itself the explanation; the concentration is high because the DDT from all the prey eaten is retained in a much smaller mass of bird tissue, and this step-up occurs at every trophic level.

mcqs.q: Why does mercury released from industry reach high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna?
options: Large fish swallow the greatest volume of water while feeding, so they take in more mercury than smaller fish do.
Mercury taken in with prey is retained in tissues rather than excreted, so its concentration rises at each trophic level up to the tuna.
Tuna swim through polluted water for years and absorb mercury through their gills rather than from their food.
Tuna live for many years, so they accumulate mercury over time; smaller fish would reach the same level if they lived as long.
mcqs.specStatementText: Biomagnification: DDT and mercury
mcqs.explain: This is biomagnification. Mercury in water and sediments is converted by bacteria to methylmercury, which is taken up by small organisms, retained rather than excreted and passed on at increasing concentration along the food chain, so long-lived top predators such as tuna carry the highest concentrations.
rationales: A student who thinks the top consumer simply takes in more picks this. The concentration in tuna comes from mercury already concentrated in the prey fish it eats, not from the water it swallows.

This is biomagnification. Mercury in water and sediments is converted by bacteria to methylmercury, which is taken up by small organisms, retained rather than excreted and passed on at increasing concentration along the food chain, so long-lived top predators such as tuna carry the highest concentrations.
A student who thinks uptake is direct from the environment picks this. Uptake across the gills is minor; the high concentration comes from eating prey that already contain methylmercury.

A student who equates biomagnification with lifetime accumulation picks this. Age contributes, but a tuna's food is itself already more concentrated than the water, and each trophic level adds a further step.

mcqs.q: Which statement about plastic pollution of the oceans is correct?
options: Marine bacteria biodegrade plastics, but so slowly that the material persists for a few decades before disappearing.
Microplastics are too small to harm marine animals, so only macroplastics have effects on marine life.
Macroplastics fragment into microplastics but are not broken down by decomposers, so the material persists.
Microplastics enter the oceans only as manufactured particles such as microbeads, not from larger plastic items.
mcqs.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
mcqs.explain: Plastics are non-biodegradable, because decomposers lack enzymes that can break down these synthetic polymers. Sunlight and waves fragment items into microplastics, but the plastic remains in the environment and enters food chains.
rationales: A student who thinks plastics decompose slowly picks this. Fragmentation is a physical process; the polymer is not decomposed, which is why plastic persists for centuries and is found in the tissues of marine organisms.

A student who equates harm with entanglement or blockage picks this. Microplastics are ingested by filter feeders and zooplankton, damage the gut, carry adsorbed pollutants and pass along food chains.

Plastics are non-biodegradable, because decomposers lack enzymes that can break down these synthetic polymers. Sunlight and waves fragment items into microplastics, but the plastic remains in the environment and enters food chains.
A student who associates microplastics only with microbeads picks this. Most microplastic comes from the fragmentation of macroplastics such as bags, bottles and nets.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the approach used to restore native forest at Hinewai Reserve in New Zealand?
options: Grazing livestock were removed and introduced gorse was left as a nurse canopy, under which native trees regenerated with minimal interference.
Native tree seedlings were raised in nurseries and planted across the whole reserve in place of the former pasture and scrub.
The introduced gorse was cleared with herbicide and machinery before native forest was allowed to return to the area.
Native forest was allowed to recover in scattered small patches across the peninsula, since connecting habitats over one large area is not needed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
mcqs.explain: Hinewai's approach is minimal interference: with livestock gone and introduced browsers controlled, native seedlings grew up through the shade-intolerant gorse, overtopped it and formed native forest without planting.
rationales: Hinewai's approach is minimal interference: with livestock gone and introduced browsers controlled, native seedlings grew up through the shade-intolerant gorse, overtopped it and formed native forest without planting.
A student who thinks rewilding means planting picks this. At Hinewai the forest regenerated naturally from seed once the human impacts that suppressed it were removed.
A student who thinks invasive plants must always be removed picks this. The gorse was deliberately left; it sheltered native seedlings and died out once they shaded it.

A student who thinks total area is all that matters picks this. Hinewai is managed as one continuous, expanding area of more than 1000 hectares; re-establishing connectivity over a large area is one of the methods of rewilding.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a method used in rewilding to restore natural processes in an ecosystem?
options: Removing apex predators from the area so that the populations of herbivores and other prey species can increase in size.
Re-establishing connectivity between areas of habitat over a large region so that animals can move between them.
Replanting the whole area with nursery-grown trees and maintaining it by continuous intensive management.
Protecting several small separate reserves instead of one large area, since total area matters more than connection.
mcqs.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
mcqs.explain: Re-establishment of connectivity of habitats over large areas is one of the methods the guide lists, alongside reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species and minimization of human impact.
rationales: A student who thinks predators reduce biodiversity picks this. Rewilding reintroduces apex predators, because as keystone species they restore the natural control of herbivores and allow vegetation and dependent species to recover.

Re-establishment of connectivity of habitats over large areas is one of the methods the guide lists, alongside reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species and minimization of human impact.
A student who equates restoration with planting picks this. Rewilding minimizes human impact so that natural regeneration and natural processes maintain the ecosystem.

A student who thinks isolated fragments are as good as a connected area picks this. Rewilding re-establishes connectivity over large areas so that populations can move, interbreed and support wide-ranging species such as apex predators.

mcqs.q: Alder trees colonising ground exposed by a retreating glacier have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules. Within decades the soil nitrogen content rises and spruce trees, which cannot grow on the bare ground, replace the alders. Which statement about the cause of this change is correct?
options: It is an abiotic cause, because only changes in the physical environment such as glacial retreat can drive succession.
The alders enriched the soil in order to prepare the site for the spruce trees that follow them in the succession.
It is a biotic cause: the alders changed the soil so that other species could establish and then outcompete them.
This is secondary succession, because soil had already formed on the site before the spruce trees arrived.
mcqs.specStatementText: Succession and what triggers it
mcqs.explain: Succession can be triggered by biotic factors as well as abiotic ones. The alders enrich the soil with nitrogen as a consequence of their symbiosis; the enriched soil allows spruce to establish, and spruce then shade out the alders.
rationales: A student who thinks succession has only abiotic causes picks this. The glacial retreat exposed the ground, but the replacement of alder by spruce was driven by the alders' effect on the soil, a biotic factor.
A student who thinks succession is purposeful picks this. Nitrogen fixation benefits the alders themselves; soil enrichment is a side effect that happens to favour their competitors.

Succession can be triggered by biotic factors as well as abiotic ones. The alders enrich the soil with nitrogen as a consequence of their symbiosis; the enriched soil allows spruce to establish, and spruce then shade out the alders.
A student who applies the soil test to each stage picks this. The sequence began on bare ground with no soil, so the whole sequence, including the spruce stage, is primary succession.

mcqs.q: Surveys were made on land exposed by a retreating glacier 10, 50, 100 and 200 years earlier. Mean plant height was 0.1 m, 3 m, 15 m and 30 m; the number of plant species was 6, 18, 25 and 31; and net primary production (kg m⁻² yr⁻¹) was 0.05, 0.4, 0.9 and 1.2. Soil depth and organic content increased throughout. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: The rise in species number is misleading, because the hardy pioneer community at 10 years was the most diverse stage.
Net primary production should have fallen after 100 years because mature trees grow slowly, so the 200-year value must be wrong.
The site surveyed at 10 years must already have had a proper soil, since plants cannot colonise ground until soil is present.
Plant size, species diversity and primary production all increased as the primary succession proceeded.
mcqs.specStatementText: What changes as primary succession proceeds
mcqs.explain: All three measures rise steadily across the sequence, as the guide describes for primary succession: larger plants, more species and greater primary production as soil builds up and nutrient cycling increases.
rationales: A student who thinks pioneers are the most diverse picks this. The data show only 6 species at 10 years and 31 at 200 years; diversity increases as habitats and food webs become more complex.

A student who confuses the growth rate of individual trees with production per square metre picks this. A forest has far more photosynthetic tissue than a pioneer community, so its production is higher.

A student who thinks soil must pre-exist picks this. The survey reports that soil depth and organic content increased through the sequence, showing that soil formed during succession, beginning with pioneers on bare ground.

All three measures rise steadily across the sequence, as the guide describes for primary succession: larger plants, more species and greater primary production as soil builds up and nutrient cycling increases.

mcqs.q: On a heather moor, heather plants pass through pioneer, building, mature and degenerate phases. In the degenerate phase the central branches die, opening a gap that is colonised by lichens and mosses before heather seedlings re-establish there. What does this show?
options: The community follows a cycle of phases driven by the heather's own ageing, rather than settling into one unchanging climax.
The moor has not yet reached its climax, which will be a permanent heather community with no gaps in it.
The repeated dying back of the heather shows that the ecosystem is unstable and is degrading towards collapse.
Each change of phase must be triggered by an external abiotic disturbance such as fire, frost or a drought.
mcqs.specStatementText: Some ecosystems cycle instead of settling
mcqs.explain: This is cyclical succession. The ecosystem persists, but its communities cycle: ageing heather opens gaps, other species occupy them, and heather re-establishes, so there is no single fixed climax community.
rationales: This is cyclical succession. The ecosystem persists, but its communities cycle: ageing heather opens gaps, other species occupy them, and heather re-establishes, so there is no single fixed climax community.
A student who expects every succession to end in a single permanent climax picks this. The cycle repeats indefinitely; the moor's stable state is the cycle itself, not a gap-free end point.
A student who reads change as instability picks this. Heather moorland has persisted through many such cycles; the degenerate phase is a normal part of the pattern, not a sign of collapse.
A student who thinks only abiotic events cause succession picks this. The cycle is driven by a biotic factor, the ageing and die-back of the heather plants themselves.

mcqs.q: Sheep have grazed a hillside for centuries and it is covered by grassland. When grazing was stopped on a fenced plot, shrubs appeared within ten years and young trees within twenty. What does this show?
options: Grassland is the natural climax community here, and fencing disturbed it and began a new succession.
Grazing had arrested succession, holding the hillside at a grassland stage below its climax community.
The shrubs and trees must have been planted, because succession cannot resume once it has been arrested by human activity.
The fence altered the plot's climate, and only such an abiotic change can make a community change.
mcqs.specStatementText: Climax communities and how humans arrest succession
mcqs.explain: Under the environmental conditions of the hillside, succession tends towards woodland. Grazing livestock remove tree and shrub seedlings, which is a human influence that prevents the climax from developing; when it stops, succession resumes.
rationales: A student who equates a long-standing community with a climax picks this. The grassland persisted only because grazing removed woody seedlings; the appearance of shrubs and trees once grazing stopped shows the climax lies beyond grassland.

Under the environmental conditions of the hillside, succession tends towards woodland. Grazing livestock remove tree and shrub seedlings, which is a human influence that prevents the climax from developing; when it stops, succession resumes.

A student who thinks arrested succession is permanent picks this. Arrested succession is maintained only while the influence continues; removing the sheep allowed seedlings to survive and succession to resume naturally.

A student who thinks succession has only abiotic causes picks this. The fence changed nothing about the climate; it removed a biotic influence, grazing, which had been preventing woody plants from establishing.

mcqs.q: How does drainage of a wetland for agriculture affect ecological succession there?
options: The drained farmland is now the climax community for the new, drier conditions, so no further succession is possible there.
The wetland community cannot re-establish afterwards, because succession stops permanently once the wetland has been drained.
It prevents the community that the wet conditions would naturally lead to from developing, so the land stays as farmland.
It starts a new succession that will lead back to the same wetland climax once the crops are harvested, since the climax for an area is fixed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Climax communities and how humans arrest succession
mcqs.explain: Drainage of wetlands is the guide's second example of a human influence that prevents a climax community from developing. The community that the waterlogged conditions would have produced is replaced by farmland that persists only while drainage and cultivation continue.
rationales: A student who thinks any persistent community is a climax picks this. Farmland is maintained by continued drainage and cultivation, not by the environment alone, so it is an arrested stage, not a climax.
A student who thinks arrested succession is irreversible picks this. When drainage is stopped and the land re-wets, wetland communities return, as wetland restoration projects have shown.

Drainage of wetlands is the guide's second example of a human influence that prevents a climax community from developing. The community that the waterlogged conditions would have produced is replaced by farmland that persists only while drainage and cultivation continue.

A student who thinks every area has one fixed climax it must return to picks this. The climax depends on the environmental conditions; while the land is kept drained the waterlogged conditions that produced the wetland community no longer exist, so succession is held at farmland and cannot lead to the wetland climax.

mcqs.q: A farm sprays insecticide and herbicide several times each season. Downstream, insect and amphibian numbers have fallen and residues of the sprays are found in well water. Which factor affecting the sustainability of agriculture do these observations illustrate?
options: Supply of inputs, since the sprays are inputs that protect the crop yield and so make the farm more sustainable.
Pollution due to agrochemicals, since the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and contaminated water beyond the farm.
Leaching of nutrients, since sprays act only on pests within the field, so the downstream losses must be due to fertilizer.
Carbon footprint, since the only effect of agrochemicals beyond the field is from the fuel burned by the machinery that sprays them.
mcqs.specStatementText: What makes farming unsustainable
mcqs.explain: Insecticides and herbicides are agrochemicals. The fall in downstream insects and amphibians and the residues in well water show that the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and polluted water off the farm, which is the pollution factor the guide lists.
rationales: A student who sees inputs only as benefits picks this. Supply of inputs is a sustainability factor because producing and applying them has costs; here the observations show damage caused by the inputs, which is pollution due to agrochemicals.

Insecticides and herbicides are agrochemicals. The fall in downstream insects and amphibians and the residues in well water show that the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and polluted water off the farm, which is the pollution factor the guide lists.

A student who thinks pesticides act only on the target pests within the field picks this. No fertilizer is mentioned; the residues in the well water are from the sprays, and insecticides and herbicides kill many non-target species when they drift, run off or leach from the field.

A student who thinks the impact of agrochemicals is only the fuel used to apply them picks this. Carbon footprint concerns greenhouse gas emissions; the observations describe toxic effects on organisms and contamination of water, which is pollution due to agrochemicals.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D4.2 Stability and change
